Hope and a future.
Head of School’s Welcome
Welcome to The Bridge, an independent Social, Emotional and Mental Health School welcoming students who have struggled to access a mainstream setting, offering them hope and most importantly, a future.
At The Bridge, wellbeing is placed at the heart of everything we do. We specialise in providing a nurturing environment that focuses on building confidence and resilience, empowering each student to reach their full academic potential and thrive in all aspects of life.
As Head of School, I am dedicated to creating a community of inclusivity, empathy and growth. Our team of highly trained staff are committed to creating a safe and supportive community where every student feels valued, respected and inspired to succeed. With small class sizes and an exciting variety of extra-curricular opportunities, students are given the tools to grow and develop a brighter future for themselves. Our aim at Key Stage 3 is to successfully re-integrate students back to a suitable mainstream setting whereas Key Stage 4 students will usually stay and complete their GCSEs with us.
Whether you are a parent, carer or student, I encourage you to explore the website and discover the many ways in which The Bridge can support your child to re-engage with their learning journey.
Maria Jackson
Head of School and Safeguarding Lead

Our Vision
Hope and a Future
At The Bridge our vision is to provide a sense of hope and an optimism about the future for every one of our pupils.
Our Mission
Our aim is that every child and young person we work with develops a sense of hope so that they can effectively face the future. Whatever challenges and difficulties they have faced in the past and whatever their feelings about the things that have happened to them, we help them to develop a sense of self worth and purpose. Every pupil is given tools to help them cope with their feelings and emotions. They develop an awareness that however difficult the challenges are, they are not permanent, personal or all pervasive, and can be overcome. Our academic curriculum is supported by a range of enrichment subjects and activities which assist them. In this way, The Bridge ensures that every pupil has the emotional, social, academic and spiritual strength and awareness to face a bright future.
Our 6 Principles – The Unique Me
To reflect the creation of our highly successful mission statement of Hope and a Future, the school embarked upon creating a set of principles, which advocates:
The Bridge believes and promotes a culture of supportive relationships that allows staff to gain the trust of our most vulnerable students. Student wellbeing is at the heart of everything we do, as we aim to develop the character of all of our students. We strongly believe The Bridge has a responsibility to ensure our students leave the setting ready and fit for life.
Our six principles are integral to achieving our goal, and play a key role in supporting students to become confident, resilient, young adult learners, as well as preparing them for their future life journey.
These six principles underpin The Unique Me, which serves to foster diversity, and is in keeping with our beliefs, that despite life’s setbacks, all students can achieve their personal goals, and build harmonious relationships within school and the wider community.
Is to know and understand your purpose in life.
Knowing Myself
Lifelong Learning
Developing Healthy Habits
Being Financially Aware
Connecting to Others
Finding a Fulfilling Future
Knowing Myself
At the Bridge we believe there is significant worth to exploring different ways our individual beliefs and thought processes vary from each other. Getting to really know ourselves helps us all to have a clear understanding of our life goals.
We believe knowing ourselves gives us greater clarity into our own personal strengths and weaknesses. This is something the school explores in many ways, one of those ways is through the C Me Profiling.
Colour Me Profiling provides students with information about their preferred way of doing things. This tool is designed to spark helpful conversations and discussions, and assists each of us to learn more about ourselves and each other.
We strongly believe there is merit to realising what is UNIQUE and what is universal. Exploring this value allows our students to become more tolerant as they begin to see the view point of others.
“He who knows others is wise. He who knows himself is enlightened.” Lao Tzu
Lifelong Learning
It is said that lifelong learning can support everyone to achieve personal fulfilment and satisfaction. That is why here at The Bridge we encourage all of our students to recognise their own personal interests and goals. We champion lifelong learning by instilling in our students that lifelong learning is about them and not what others want them to do or be.
One of the examples of this, is the Unique Me Project which all students undertake when they start at The Bridge. This project allows students to explore topics which they may have a passion for, or a particular interest in pursuing when they leave school, or it may be a dream goal.
We believe, if students are able to recognise and explore their personal interests and goals they will be inspired to attempt the “new” and go on to achieve in life. Students are often inspired by their Unique Me Projects, as they are the ones in control, and it allows them the time to discover new personal interests which re-ignites their passion for learning.
Developing Healthy Habits
What is a habit? A habit is something that is routine to the individual, which is repeated often without knowing it.
The Bridge recognises that good healthy habits are beneficial to improving both physical and mental well-being. The school works hard with students to develop their understanding of the importance of healthy habits. With this in mind, the school has created a programme of activities and workshops which focus on cultivating routines in key areas of everyday life.
Through dedicated workshops, activities and the school’s extensive PSHCE programme the school is able to support and promote the benefits of healthy habits.
The areas of focus are:
Healthy Relationships – Keeping Connected
Across the school’s curriculum and through our Thought of the Week programme, students are consistently exposed to the virtues of adopting healthy habits.
The Bridge believes:
“We are what we REPEATEDLY DO. Success is not an action but a habit.” – Aristotle
Being Financially Aware
Financial literacy is important to us all and teaching financial literacy helps our students understand money and budgeting. It is proven that appreciation for finances and good financial planning alleviates stress and subsequently leads to better health outcomes.
Good financial awareness and astuteness will open up more options for our students, which will allow for greater freedom of choice in future life.
Connecting to Others
Definition of communication:To convey knowledge of or information about
Definition of connecting: To place or establish in relationship
It is important that our students not only learn how to communicate with those around them, but more importantly, grow in confidence so they are genuinely able to make a connection with others.
To be able to connect to individuals is highly effective and requires skill and purpose and is arguably more genuine than just communicating. To have a connection is to have the ability for that moment in time to make a leap into the other person’s world.
Fostering good connections is a skill which will help develop our student’s social skills as well as preparing them for later in life. The skill of connecting to others is especially vital in a world of social media and texting, where individuals communicate without speaking or feeling. It is important to note that communicating is not connecting, as highlighted in the definition above.
At The Bridge we trust and value what is going on in our community, as well as in our peers and colleagues lives. To know what our peers and colleagues are going through, and to support them through their difficulties underpins the strength of building good relationships. Personal Development and Welfare is at the heart of everything we do and stand for here at The Bridge, being able to effectively deliver this requires a strong connection to others and from others.
It is often stated that “the greatest leaders are the ones that connect with individuals.”
Finding a Fulfilling Future
We encourage all of our students to have belief in their own future. The school’s mission statement of Hope and a Future is the foundation of everything we do at The Bridge.
We are advocates of being your own person and most importantly, to face our fears in order that we can move forward in life.
Each day we support and encourage our students to overcome obstacles and accept that taking a leap of faith and “doing” may not always be easy and smooth sailing, but nor is it the hardest obstacle they have ever had to face.
Through trust and support we nurture and teach our students to do those things that matter, which will also make a positive difference to their lives
The school’s Life Coach is an integral part of the school support system, where students are allowed the time to embrace their uniqueness and enhance their personal skill sets, so they are able to face their future with confidence.
Our six principles are intrinsically linked, receive high priority within the school, and are pivotal to the school curriculum; incorporated in school events, extra-curricular clubs and workshops held at The Bridge. Our ethos is strong, clear, and reflected in everything we do, the language we use, and the examples we set.

Art & Design at The Bridge
Aims and Objectives
Aligned with the National Curriculum for Art & Design, our curriculum at The Bridge empowers students to develop practical skills, experiment with diverse media, and create meaningful, personal works of art. Students engage with a broad spectrum of historical and contemporary artistic practices, learning to critically evaluate both their own work and that of others.
We aim to equip students with the skills to:
Students follow a broad, skills-based pathway at Key Stage 3 (KS3), with the majority progressing to GCSE Art & Design at Key Stage 4 (KS4). Beyond subject mastery, the Art curriculum actively supports cross-curricular learning alongside students’ spiritual, moral, social, and cultural (SMSC) development.
Teaching and Learning Styles
We employ a dynamic range of teaching methodologies, including teacher-led demonstrations, guided discussions, practical workshops, written annotations, and self-directed inquiries.
Art and Design Curriculum Planning and Provision
Because students enter The Bridge at varied entry points with diverse prior educational experiences, our curriculum planning remains flexible yet structured. The KS3 framework builds a foundational skill set designed for seamless transition into KS4 GCSE Art & Design.
Year 8 Curriculum
Core Objectives & Focus Areas
• To create tone using pencil and develop observational drawing skills.
• To refine drawing techniques and tonal shading proficiency.
• To understand fundamental colour theory, mixing primary, secondary, and tertiary colours.
• To identify complementary pairs and define warm and cool tones for balanced schemes.
• To understand structural principles of patterns (symmetry, asymmetry, repeat grids).
• To analyse and compare global pattern traditions across cultures and media.
Architectural Letters
• To explore typography and imagery linked to the theme of personal identity.
• To translate 2D designs into 3D forms using modeling and construction techniques.
• To evaluate and adapt designs iteratively throughout the fabrication process.
Year 9 Curriculum
Core Objectives & Focus Areas
• To explore the Pop Art movement (Roy Lichtenstein, Maria Qamar, Keith Haring) and replicate traits like Ben-Day dots and graphic outlines.
• To compose original responses layering commercial imagery, typography, and graffiti styles.
• To demonstrate control in watercolor and ink application using vibrant primary palettes.
• To critically analyse progress in tracing, color theory, and composition.
• To develop fine motor precision experimenting with collage, mixed media, and mosaic construction.
• To analyse established artists using specific technical art vocabulary.
• To enhance observational accuracy in sketchbooks and build confidence through self-evaluation.
• To investigate the cultural context and aesthetics of African masks and their global influence.
• To analyse Chief Jimoh Buraimoh’s bead painting techniques versus traditional mask-making.
• To build 3D cardboard relief structures and apply decorative surface treatments.
• To study screen printing history (Warhol, Banksy, Fairey) and master stencil integrity (bridges/islands).
• To practice color mixing, layer registration, and multi-layer alignment.
• To design and produce a high-quality print outcome linked to LGBTQ+ Pride Month.
Year 10 Curriculum (GCSE)
• To document discovery through primary research (trips) and artist analysis (Paula Swisher, Angela Faustina, Rachel Newling, Irene Meneconi, Beth Cavener, Andreas Pries).
• To master specialist techniques: biro on text, tonal work on black paper, etching, and watercolor.
• To demonstrate observational accuracy, culminating in a refined outcome for a 5-hour mock exam.
• To investigate portraiture evolution (museum visits) and study key artists (Shirin Neshat, Bruno Delzou, Chuck Close, Maurizio Anzeri, Boris Nzebo, Oscar Ukonu).
• To conduct media trials across pencil, watercolor, pastel, and digital manipulation.
• To explore identity narrative, lighting, and composition through self-portraits and photo studies.
Year 11 Curriculum (GCSE Examination Year)
Core Objectives & Focus Areas
Unit 1: Personal Portfolio
• Complete personal portfolio of work, consolidating advanced skills in chosen media.
• Conclude Unit 1 with a 5-hour mock examination by December.
Unit 2: Externally Set Task
• Develop individual responses to an exam-board theme (released in January).
• Refine critical analysis, independent research, and preparatory studies.
• Complete the final 10-hour practical examination under controlled conditions.
Cross-Curricular Links
Art & Design integrates with broader school initiatives and academic subjects to enrich learning:
Teaching Art to Students with Special Needs
At The Bridge, Art is accessible to all students at KS3 and KS4 regardless of baseline ability. Learning opportunities are tailored to individual needs, supporting both more able students and those with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND).
Planning, delivery, and feedback strictly align with each student’s Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) and Individual Education Plan (IEP). Flexible scheduling forms part of a bespoke timetable negotiated with the Headteacher to ensure every student thrives.
Assessment, Recording, and Reporting
Assessment is continuous, combining formative, summative, and peer approaches:

English at The Bridge
Aims and Objectives
The English curriculum at The Bridge is underpinned by the school’s ethos, “Hope and a Future”, and by its values of courageous optimism, boundless creativity and heartfelt compassion.
Students may join The Bridge at different points in the academic year and with varied prior experiences of English. Interrupted attendance, unmet special educational needs and previous difficulties engaging with education may have created gaps in knowledge, skills and confidence. The English curriculum therefore provides a strong and nurturing core that is responsive to students’ starting points, attendance patterns, interests and wellbeing needs.
The curriculum aims to develop confident readers, writers, speakers and listeners. Students build increasingly secure knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, literary methods, text structures and social and historical contexts. They revisit and apply this knowledge across literature, fiction, non-fiction, spoken language and writing for different audiences and purposes.
Talk is central to English. Students develop ideas through paired discussion, debate, role-play, questioning and formal presentation. They also learn to listen actively, respond respectfully and recognise that texts and issues can support more than one reasoned interpretation.
Teaching and Learning
Teaching is designed to foster curiosity, confidence and trust. Students encounter challenging texts and ideas through appropriate scaffolding, modelling, retrieval, guided practice and opportunities for independent application. Emphasis is placed on approaches in which students are as active as possible in their learning. Students work individually, in pairs, or as a whole class. Sometimes students select their own groups, but sometimes, according to the aims of the activity, groupings will be constructed to create productive dynamics within groups, or to ensure a mixture of ability, to allow for differentiation, or gender. Talk is recognized as being of central importance in the classroom: rooms are arranged to encourage collaborative work and peer support. Students at The Bridge have enjoyed many a debate on contemporary issues but are also used to working with minimal talk, when necessary.As well as celebrating student achievement through assessment, students’ creative outputs are celebrated through wall displays, booklets of shared prose and poetry, end of term reward certificates, and biannual reports to parent/carers.
Students are encouraged to celebrate special literary/mental health events such as National Poetry Day, World Book Day and World Mental Health Day and to enter film review writing competitions. The department organises visits to the theatre, as well as theatre and Speak Out Challenge workshops. These visits give students the opportunity to see productions and consolidate learning relevant to their work in English. They are also used to encourage students to develop an interest in theatre-going and the spoken word for its own sake, and to interact with other students and staff in a way not possible in school.
English Curriculum Planning and Provision
KS3 English
The Key Stage 3 curriculum provides an engaging and supportive foundation in reading, writing and spoken language. Students encounter fiction, non-fiction, poetry and drama from different periods, cultures and perspectives. The curriculum develops the knowledge, skills and confidence students need for continued secondary study, possible reintegration back into a mainstream school setting, and later qualification pathways.
KS3 Curriculum Overview
Autumn term: identity, voice and belonging
Students explore how writers present identity, belonging, aspiration and cultural experience.
Possible content includes:
Emotional-literacy opportunities include exploring identity, aspiration, belonging, difference and respectful responses to experiences other than one’s own.
Cross-curricular connections may include history, citizenship, geography, music and PSHE.
Spring term: power, influence and choices
Students explore how language can influence behaviour, relationships and public opinion.
Possible content includes:
Contemporary non-fiction topics might include social media and wellbeing, environmental responsibility, artificial intelligence and misinformation, equality, education or community life.
Core learning includes understanding writers’ viewpoints, recognising bias, analysing rhetorical choices, developing arguments, using evidence and adapting register to audience and purpose.
Emotional-literacy opportunities include recognising influence and pressure, considering motives, disagreeing respectfully and examining how characters manage conflict and choices.
Cross-curricular connections may include drama, history, computing, media literacy, citizenship, science and PSHE.
Summer term: society, responsibility and change
Students explore how literature and non-fiction represent communities, conflict, responsibility and social change.
Possible content includes:
Emotional-literacy opportunities include considering fairness, responsibility, courage, relationships and the consequences of personal and collective decisions.
Cross-curricular connections may include history, politics and citizenship, geography, ethics, careers and the arts.

KS4 English
At Key Stage 4, students follow an appropriate pathway leading to GCSE English Language and, where agreed, GCSE English Literature. Where a Functional Skills pathway is more appropriate, it provides a distinct, purposeful route focused on communication for everyday life, education and employment.
Qualification Pathways
GCSE English Language
GCSE English Language is the principal English qualification pathway at Key Stage 4. Students develop critical reading, comparison, evaluation, creative and transactional writing, technical accuracy, and spoken-language skills. Teaching prepares students for AQA GCSE English Language 8700, including Paper 1, Paper 2 and the separately reported Spoken Language endorsement.
GCSE English Literature
GCSE English Literature is a separate qualification with its own prescribed content and assessment requirements. Students study a Shakespeare play, a nineteenth-century novel, a modern prose or drama text, the AQA poetry anthology and unseen poetry. Entry decisions are made through the school’s agreed curriculum and assessment processes and should take account of each student’s entitlement, prior learning and individual circumstances.
Functional Skills English
Functional Skills English is an alternative qualification pathway where this has been agreed as appropriate. It develops reading, writing, speaking, listening and communication in purposeful contexts connected with everyday life, further education and employment. It is not simply a reduced version of GCSE English Language, and its content and assessment requirements are taught explicitly.
Students learn through a balanced range of teacher explanation, modelling, supported reading, discussion, collaborative activity, deliberate practice and independent application. Groupings and levels of support are selected according to the needs of individual students.
Relevant contemporary topics may include:
Texts and topics are reviewed regularly so that they remain relevant, age-appropriate and suitable for the particular cohort.
Students compose, edit and present work using handwriting and appropriate digital tools. They develop word-processing, proofreading, research, source-evaluation and presentation skills.

KS4 Curriculum Overview
Macbeth—plot, character, themes, dramatic methods, contextual understanding and analytical writing.
GCSE English Language Paper 1 foundations—fiction reading, inference, language and structural analysis, evaluation, descriptive and narrative writing.
Assessment: baseline evidence followed by focused Literature and Language assessments.

GCSE English Language Paper 2 foundations—non-fiction and literary non-fiction, summary, comparison, analysis of viewpoints and transactional writing.
Assessment: poetry analysis/comparison and selected Paper 2 tasks.
Completion and consolidation of Power and Conflict; unseen-poetry reading and comparison; Literature assessment.
Interleaved Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice; Spoken Language preparation where appropriate; Language assessment.
End-of-Year 10 examinations followed by feedback and gap analysis.
Completion or consolidation of the remaining Literature components according to the cohort’s prior coverage. Current teaching priorities include Macbeth and the Power and Conflict anthology.
Planned retrieval and revision of previously studied texts, including The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and An Inspector Calls, where these form part of the cohort’s examination course.
English Language Paper 1 and Paper 2 practice, informed by diagnostic assessment.
Spoken Language completion for any student who has not yet secured an outcome.
Structured revision of all examination texts and poetry.

Mock examinations, feedback, question-level analysis and targeted reteaching.

English also provides planned opportunities to develop emotional literacy. Through characters, speakers and viewpoints, students explore emotions, motivations, relationships, choices, consequences and different perspectives. Teachers model respectful disagreement and precise emotional vocabulary.
Emotional-literacy opportunities support engagement with the English curriculum; they do not replace its subject-specific knowledge and skills.
Poetry Pharmacy
The Bridge Poetry Pharmacy provides opportunities for students to read, discuss and create poetry connected with themes such as anxiety, difference, loneliness, courage, hope and belonging. Students may draw upon literary texts, observation, imagination or experience, but are never required to disclose personal information. Themes and activities are selected sensitively in accordance with students’ needs and safeguarding considerations. The unit develops vocabulary, empathy, creativity, interpretation and confidence in communicating ideas.
Cross-Curricular Links
Cross-curricular links are selected where they strengthen understanding of English rather than distract from the subject’s curriculum aims. These may include:
Cross-curricular connection
History: monarchy, Jacobean society and beliefs; Drama: performance and stagecraft; PSHE: ambition, influence, guilt and decision-making
Power and Conflict poetry
History: war, empire and migration; Geography: place, identity and environment; Art: imagery and representation
Science: nineteenth-century scientific development; History: Victorian society; PSHE: identity, reputation and responsibility
History: Edwardian society and social class; Citizenship: inequality and collective responsibility; Drama: staging and dramatic tension
Art and media: visual stimuli; Drama: voice and character; PSHE: empathy and perspective
Citizenship and media literacy: argument, bias, evidence and misinformation; Science and Geography: communicating public issues
Citizenship: reasoned debate; Careers: presentation and interview skills; Computing: responsible research and presentation
Careers, financial awareness, workplace communication and everyday information
Teaching English to Students with Special Needs
In English, specific teaching approaches including grouping, resource, and work differentiated by outcome and task, are used to cater for the diverse academic, social and emotional needs of our students; all are provided with learning opportunities to achieve at their own level, including those who may be very able, have English as an additional language, or who have specific learning difficulties. When planning and delivering English and providing feedback to students, any EHCP (Educational, Health and Care Plan), IEP (Individual Educational Plan) and SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) are taken into account.
Assessment, Recording and Reporting
Assessment is used to identify what students know, what they can apply independently and what requires further teaching. Assessment in English includes retrieval, questioning, discussion, short analytical responses, extended writing, live feedback, self-reflection, end-of-unit tasks, mock examinations and end-of-year examinations. An appropriate combination of formative and summative evidence is used. GCSE work is assessed with reference to the relevant AQA assessment objectives. Assessment information is used to identify gaps caused by interrupted attendance, plan reteaching and provide appropriate stretch. Mathematics at The Bridge
Aims and objectives
All students at the Bridge are prepared for their final GCSE Mathematics examination in Year 11. Whilst recognizing the individual needs of our students and knowledge gaps, we provide them with a Mathematics Curriculum that parallels practice in mainstream schools and give them consistent expectations in a Mathematics lesson. We follow The Bridge ethos of Hope and a Future and aim to inspire a positive attitude and confidence in all our students. Delivery of the curriculum fulfils the Unique Me characteristics we wish every student to develop during their time with us, aiming to equip our students with the following skills –
Teaching and Learning
We use a range of teaching and learning styles. The teacher explains and models the topic that is being taught, addressing misconceptions and assessing for learning. The nature of students at The Bridge is that they come from different schools which follow different curriculums as well as experiencing significant periods of absence. All gaps are acknowledged and individual interventions are planned. Classes have a maximum of eight students to encourage full participation in discussion and enable individualised learning to take place. PSHE at The Bridge
Aims and objectives
Throughout their time at The Bridge, all students undertake a programme of Personal, Social, Health and Economic education. Our PSHE education programme is underpinned by The Bridge ethos of Hope and a Future and fulfils the Unique Me characteristics we wish every student to develop during their time with us, aiming to equip our students with the following skills –
Teaching and learning styles
We use a range of teaching and learning styles including discussions, case studies, investigations, witness statements, presentations, project work, games and problem-solving activities. We encourage students to take part in a range of practical activities that promote active citizenship, e.g. charity fundraising, the planning of school special events such as World Mental Health Day, enterprise, or involvement in an activity to help other individuals or groups less fortunate than themselves. Classes have a maximum of eight students to encourage full participation in discussion and enable individualised learning to take place. Students have multiple opportunities to participate in workshops delivered by external providers throughout the year where they have the chance to meet and work with members of the community, such as health workers, police, and subject specialists. Regular trips are organised to further support the delivery of the curriculum. “The Unique Me” is a student-led project focusing on a chosen interest or, in Year 11, an aspiration for future work or further study and developed throughout the year to encourage important skills such as research, independence, critical thinking and expression. Where applicable, the project involves a practical element relevant to the chosen area of interest.
PSHE planning
PSHE is not a stand-alone subject and has many cross curricular links with all other subjects taught at The Bridge eg; modules such as Keeping Safe and Healthy are linked with Food lessons and Social Media with ICT lessons. Dedicated one hour PSHE lessons are taught twice weekly across all year groups. We also develop PSHE and Citizenship through activities and whole school events eg; celebrating key events throughout the year such as Remembrance Day, Thought for the Week and promoting key topics such as First Aid etc.Modules covered are –
Emotional WellbeingKeeping Safe and Healthy Social MediaAlcohol
Tobacco and DrugsSexual HealthRespectful Relationships Families and Parenting
Careers and your FutureFinancial ChoicesPreparing for GCSEs Study Skills
Year 7 and 8 students follow the Key Steps programme. This may vary student to student depending on their starting point at The Bridge. The following topics are covered each term –
Autumn term – Identity, Community and Health
Spring term – Citizenship, Environment, Personal Finance
Summer term – Enterprise, Values and International
Teaching PSHE to students with special needs
At The Bridge, we teach PSHE to all students, regardless of their ability. We provide learning opportunities matched to the individual needs of each student, including those who are more able or have learning difficulties. When planning and delivering PSHE and providing feedback to students, any EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan) IEP (Individual Educational Plan) and SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) are taken into account.
Incorporating Reading in the PSHE curriculum
Reading is a valuable skill for learning PSHE, as it helps students to access information, develop personal and social skills, and communicate their views. In our PSHE lessons, we incorporate reading in various ways, such as:
Comprehension task: At least, once every half term, we give students a comprehension task on a PSHE article, linked to the current area of learning. The article covers topics such as health, relationships, citizenship, or careers. Students read the article and answer questions to demonstrate their understanding and opinionsReading from the board: We encourage students to read the learning objectives, key words, and questions from the board and then discuss them in class. This helps them to focus on the lesson aims, expand their vocabulary, and engage in dialogue
Paired reading: We use information sheets when completing tasks, such as role plays, quizzes, or surveys. Students work in pairs to read the information and share their ideas. This helps them to collaborate, listen, and learn from each other
Reading debates: We expose students to different perspectives and arguments on PSHE issues, such as drugs, bullying, or democracy. Students read both sides of the debate and then discuss them in lessons. This helps them to develop critical thinking, empathy, and respect for diversity
Well-being library: We have a collection of books on topics related to well-being, such as mental health, self-esteem, or coping with stress. Students have access to the library and can borrow books to read at home or in school. This helps them to find support, inspiration, and guidance for their personal and social development
News story of the week: We post the latest PSHE news story on the board outside the science room. This is to encourage students to read while they are waiting in the corridor before lessons, breaktimes, or lunchtimes. The news story covers current events and issues that are relevant to PSHE, such as climate change, human rights, or diversity. This helps them to keep up with the world and develop their awareness and curiosity
Research tasks: We assign students research tasks that involve reading up on a subject and then completing their Unique Me projects. The subject can be anything that interests them, such as a hobby, a career, or a culture. Students use various sources, such as books, websites, or magazines, to find information and present it in a creative way. This helps them to explore their identity, interests, and aspirations
Assessment and recordingAssessment needs to value and recognise what students have done or completed successfully, thereby raising their self-esteem. Therefore, a variety of approaches to the assessment of individual achievement is used in PSHE. After introducing a topic, theory will be taught through a variety of activities. At the end of each module, each student will complete an extended writing challenge based on the module content. This may be completed individually or in pairs/groups. The challenge is then assessed using a green What Went Well (WWW) and Even Better If (EBI) sheet and time allocated to making improvements. Assessment may be self/peer or teacher based. Challenges. Achievements of pupils in PSHE are reported to parents twice yearly.
ResourcesWe use the objectives from The PSHE Association Programme of Study and the current statutory guidelines for Relationships, Sex and Health from The Department for Education to plan PSHE lessons. The Bridge has a range of books dealing with aspects of PSHE including bereavement, healthy food, sexual health and emotional wellbeing. We also have the British Heart Foundation CPR Kit including Resus Annies, a contraception kit and various health education resources. Resources are purchased regularly according to topics being studied.
Monitoring and reviewMaria Jackson (Head of School) is responsible for monitoring the standard of student work and the quality of teaching. Pip Harrington (Head of Personal Development) is responsible for the development and delivery of the PSHE curriculum. Monitoring of the PSHE curriculum and areas for development are identified as part of the School Development Plan with the Head of School and the lead governor responsible. Feedback is then given to the Local Governing Committee.

Aims and Objectives
At The Bridge, we aim to develop curious, knowledgeable and confident young scientists who are equipped with the knowledge, skills and understanding required to succeed in education and everyday life. Through the study of science, students develop an understanding of how the natural world works, the impact humans have on the environment, and the importance of evidence-based decision making.
Our curriculum is aligned with the National Curriculum for Science and is designed to support students in making successful transitions both back into mainstream education and onwards to further study.
Specifically, we aim to:
Teaching and Learning
At The Bridge, a range of teaching and learning approaches are used to deliver a knowledge-rich Science curriculum. These include:
Learning is carefully sequenced to build knowledge over time through a spiral curriculum, revisiting key concepts with increasing depth and complexity.
Where appropriate, educational visits, visiting speakers and enrichment opportunities are used to enhance students’ understanding of science and its applications in the wider world.

Retrieval practice and regular review activities

Science Curriculum Planning and Provision
At Key Stage 4, students study Biology as it is generally the most accessible of the three sciences and provides students with a strong foundation for GCSE success. The curriculum follows the AQA GCSE Biology specification and is designed to develop both scientific knowledge and examination skills.
All required practical activities from the AQA Triple Science Biology specification are completed, ensuring students gain first-hand experience of scientific investigation and practical techniques. Practical work is fully integrated into teaching and learning and supports students in developing the Working Scientifically skills assessed within GCSE Biology.
Students are provided with frequent opportunities to complete exam-style questions, retrieval activities and full examination papers throughout Key Stage 4. This structured approach ensures that students are well prepared for their GCSE examinations in Year 11 and can approach assessments with confidence.
Curriculum content may be adapted according to students’ prior learning, point of entry and individual educational needs.
At Key Stage 3, students follow a broad and balanced Science curriculum aligned with the National Curriculum. Students study Biology, Chemistry and Physics to ensure that they develop a secure foundation across all three sciences.
This approach is particularly important at The Bridge as it ensures students do not develop knowledge gaps during their placement and are able to transition successfully back into mainstream education when appropriate.

Our sports programme is underpinned by The Bridge ethos of Hope and a Future and fulfils many of the Unique Me characteristics we wish every student to develop during their time with us, aiming to equip our students with the following skills –

Statistics at The Bridge
Aims and Objectives
All students at The Bridge are prepared for their final GCSE Mathematics examination in Year 11. Those students that are more able and willing to take on extra study may be offered the opportunity to take GCSE Statistics alongside Mathematics.
The Bridge ethos of Hope and a Future aims to inspire a positive attitude and confidence towards mathematical concepts in all our students. The delivery of both the Mathematics and Statistics curriculums fulfil the Unique Me characteristics we wish every student to develop during their time with us, aiming to equip our students with essential life skills to take them forward.
The Statistics curriculum gives students the opportunity, should they desire, to explore in more detail an area of Mathematics – an area that has practical application to the world beyond education. We provide students with the necessary tools and conceptual foundations to analyse data, extract information intelligently from data given and be able to conclude and make decisions based on it. We also focus on them being able to critically assess the quality of analysis that others present to help in their decision-making process. It involves asking questions about the world and finding answers to them in a scientific way, helping to understand a subject more deeply. These skills acquired are intended to be transferable, opening up opportunities to enhance other studies or career progression.
Teaching and Learning
We use a range of teaching and learning styles. The teacher explains and models the topic that is being taught, addressing misconceptions and assessing for learning. Student gaps in learning are acknowledged and individual interventions are planned.
GCSE Statistics incorporates statistics, probability, numbers and certain elements of algebra. This links to many of the graphs, diagrams and tables used in business, scientific research and media. Students are encouraged to develop inquiring techniques enabling them to model sets of data, analyse them and justify their conclusions both statistically and in real terms. Preparation for the Statistics exam will take place in addition to normal Mathematics lesson time and the exam will be sat at the end of Year 11. GCSE Statistics will overlap with many techniques in GCSE Mathematics but will seek to bring a further breadth of understanding.
Statistics Curriculum Planning and Provision
Statistics lessons are delivered to students in parallel to the core Mathematics lessons once a week across Year 10 and Year 11. Lessons run in tandem to the Mathematics mainstream syllabus and students are assessed with an end of Year 10 exam as well as February mock exams for Year 11.
Students will learn how to plan an investigation, recognise and interpret different types of data, learn about populations and sampling techniques, data collection techniques from different sources and consider their reliability.
Students will learn about measures of central tendency (e.g. mean, median, mode, seasonal variation etc.) and measures of dispersion (e.g. interquartile range, standard deviation, calculate outliers etc.) as well as additional summary statistics (e.g. index numbers, interpret rates of change etc.) Students will analyse bi-variate data using scatter diagrams and measures of correlation (such as Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient and Pearson’s product moment correlation coefficient), interpreting their calculations in relation to the ‘real-life’ context. Students will analyse time series data, identifying trends and calculating moving averages.
Students will build on their existing knowledge regarding probability. Students will also learn about probability distributions (such as Binomial and Normal distributions) and know how to interpret characteristics of these. As part of the course, students will study the ideas behind conducting a practical investigation. This will help to build on and pull together the skills developed from the topics above.
Cross-Curricular Links
Statistics has many cross-curricular links with other subjects taught at The Bridge in particular links to Mathematics, Science, Biology and Physics. ICT lessons overlap with various presentations of data.
Skills developed and career opportunities
A career in statistics is a rewarding and often exciting career. Statisticians work with the data that are all around us and the opportunities for work are endless. Examples of Statistics Careers:
Medicine: The search for improved medical treatments rests on careful experiments that compare promising new treatments with the current state of the art. Statisticians work with medical teams to design experiments and analyse the complex data they produce.
Environment: Studies of the environment require data on the abundance and location of plants and animals, on the spread of pollution from its sources, and on the possible effects of changes in human activities. The data are often incomplete or uncertain, but statisticians can help uncover their meaning.
Industry: The future of many industries and their employees depends on improvement in the quality of goods and services and the efficiency with which they are produced and delivered. Improvement should be based on data, rather than guesswork. More companies are installing elaborate systems to collect and act on data to better serve their customers.
Government Surveys: How many people are unemployed this month? What do we export to China and what do we import? Are rates of violent crime increasing or decreasing? The government wants data on issues such as these to guide policy and government statistics agencies provide them by surveys of households and businesses.
Market Research: Are consumer tastes in television programs changing? What are promising locations for a new retail outlet? Market researchers use both government data and their own surveys to answer questions such as these. Statisticians design the elaborate surveys that gather data for both public and private use
Teaching Statistics to Students with Special Needs
At The Bridge, we teach Mathematics to all students, regardless of their ability. Statistics is an extension of this and incorporates a more detailed study of an area of Mathematics which student can find helpful and supports other cross curricular studies whilst at the same time providing for a further GCSE revisiting and extending some of the Mathematics core curriculum. When planning and delivering Mathematics and providing feedback to students, any EHCP (Educational, Health and Care Plan) IEP (Individual Educational Plan) and SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) are taken into account. At The Bridge we provide learning opportunities matched to the individual needs of each student.
Assessment, Recording and Reporting
In line with the Mathematics teaching at the Bridge, students access direct teaching of Statistics principles which is thereafter followed by practice and consolidation exercises. The teacher assesses student’s processes, applications of knowledge and understanding and provides feedback to the students within the lesson. Reviewing and assessing learning is done within each module as well as on a termly basis with the end-of-term tests. The teacher provides feedback with a What Went Well (WWW) and Even Better If (EBI) format and students improve the work or provide corrections. Assessment may be self/peer or teacher-based. The Edexcel GCSE Statistics examination consists of two exams of equal importance. Both papers are 1½ hours and focus on the same content and assessment objectives. Calculators may be used in both examinations. Achievements of students in Statistics are reported to parents twice yearly.
Department Resources
We follow the GCSE Statistics scheme of work. Differentiated resources are taken from websites such as Twinkl, Maths Made Easy, Pixi Maths, Maths Genie and TES. The Bridge has access to Pearson workbooks for Higher Level GCSE Statistics.
Governance, Monitoring and Review
Maria Jackson (Headteacher) is responsible for monitoring the standard of student work and the quality of teaching. Klara Stravs is responsible for the delivery of the Statistics curriculum. Half termly assessment is carried out according to school policy and this feeds into data drops and the school’s reports to the Local Governing Committee. The development of the Statistics curriculum is reviewed annually by the Headteacher and professional development needs are identified.

Textiles at The Bridge
Aims and Objectives
Throughout their time at The Bridge, all students study Textiles. The aims of this course are as follows:
To understand how the fabric is constructed
Teaching and Learning
A variety of teaching and learning styles are used to deliver this course. Emphasis is put on encouraging students to work independently when designing, planning and preparing their fabric for the project. Teamwork is also an important part of the production of textile items. Students will support each other with hand sewing and the use of the sewing machine. Students are supported throughout the course, particularly with the production side. The aim is to promote confidence and independence whilst giving students the opportunity to utilise these skills at home. Teacher demonstrations take place where appropriate to model correct techniques to students.
Textiles Curriculum Planning and Provision
Students come to The Bridge at different entry points and with mixed prior experience of learning in Textiles so curriculum planning in Textiles requires a flexible approach. The KS3 Textiles curriculum builds a skills base which can lead to progressing these skills at KS4.
Modules completed across the course include –
Introduction to Textiles
Basic Machine Sewing Skills
Henna enhanced with embroidery skills
Cross-Curricular Links
There are a number of cross-curricular links:
English – Reading and interpreting design briefs, following instructions, researching designers and textile products, using specialist vocabulary, presenting ideas and evaluating practical work through extended writing.
Mathematics – Measuring accurately, calculating seam allowances, scaling patterns, using ratios, recognising symmetry, interpreting data and developing precision throughout practical work.
Science – Understanding the properties of natural and synthetic fibres, colour theory and dyes (how they work).
Geography – Exploring global textile production, ethical sourcing, sustainable fashion, recycling, environmental impact and the journey of textiles from raw materials to finished products.
ICT – Independent research, digital design, creating presentations, producing mood boards, evaluating products and using software like PowerPoint and Word to present their work. PSHE – Developing resilience, confidence, creativity, teamwork, organisation, environmental responsibility and safe working practices.
Unique Me – Knowing Myself, Connecting to Others, Developing Healthy Habits, Lifelong Learning, Finding a Fulfilling Future and Being Financially Aware.
British Values – Rule of Law through following health and safety procedures; Individual Liberty through creative decision-making; Mutual Respect and Tolerance through appreciating diverse cultures, traditions and textile practices; Democracy through collaborative design discussions and teamwork; Individual Responsibility through safe, independent working and sustainable choices.
Teaching Textiles to Students with Special Needs
Depending on timetables, some students are offered the opportunity to study Textiles, regardless of their ability. We provide learning opportunities matched to the individual needs of each student, including those who are more able or have learning difficulties. When planning and delivering Textiles lessons and providing feedback to students, any EHCP (Educational, Health and Care Plan) IEP (Individual Educational Plan) and SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) are taken into account.
Department Resources
All fabrics and materials for practical Textile lessons are provided to the students free of charge. The Bridge has access to sewing machines and ICT facilities.
Assessment, Recording and Reporting
A variety of approaches to the assessment of individual achievement is used in Textiles. After introducing a topic, the theory will be taught through a variety of activities with a large practical element. Verbal feedback is given after every practical lesson and students self/peer evaluate their work to enable them to identify what was successful (WWW) and what could be improved upon (EBI) with next steps identified. Every student keeps a file of work undertaken for each module, including photographic evidence of their practical work.
Governance, Monitoring and Review
Maria Jackson (Headteacher) is responsible for monitoring the standard of student work and the quality of teaching. Raj Narwal is responsible for the development and delivery of the Textiles curriculum. The development of the Textiles curriculum is reviewed annually by the Headteacher and professional development needs are identified.

pageCache.text:
At The Bridge Primary School we aim to enable all children, including those with Special Educational Needs to engage with and enjoy a well-balanced and broad curriculum. We strongly pride ourselves in supporting children to develop as confident, individual and independent pupils.
From September 2014, every Local Authority will be required to publish information about services they expect to be available in their area for children and young people from birth to 25 years who have Special Educational Needs and/or Disabilities (SEND). All schools are to complete an SEN Information Report that will contribute to the local offer.
